description: Novelty set (plan Task 4.1). Pairs of write-ups labelled DUPLICATE (same vulnerability or technique, different source or wording) or DISTINCT (different technique, same product or platform). 'tune' pairs pick the cosine threshold; 'heldout' pairs report suppression and false-suppression rates. Texts are written in the shape the novelty check embeds: title, mechanism, impact.
labelled_by: DRAFT: needs two team members to confirm each label before results are reported

pairs.label: DUPLICATE
pairs.a: HTTP request smuggling via CL.TE desync. The front-end proxy honours Content-Length while the back-end honours Transfer-Encoding: chunked, so a crafted request leaves a prefix in the back-end socket. The prefix is prepended to the next user's request, enabling request hijacking and bypass of front-end access controls.
pairs.b: Desync attacks: front-end uses Content-Length, back-end uses chunked Transfer-Encoding. Smuggling a partial request onto the shared connection poisons the next victim's request, letting an attacker capture other users' requests and reach admin paths the front-end blocks.

pairs.label: DISTINCT
pairs.a: HTTP request smuggling via CL.TE desync. The front-end proxy honours Content-Length while the back-end honours Transfer-Encoding: chunked, so a crafted request leaves a prefix in the back-end socket, enabling request hijacking.
pairs.b: Web cache poisoning through an unkeyed X-Forwarded-Host header. The application reflects the header into script URLs, but the cache key ignores it, so one poisoned response is served to every visitor and loads attacker JavaScript.

pairs.label: DUPLICATE
pairs.a: Bypassing Android certificate pinning with Frida. Hook OkHttp3 CertificatePinner.check and the platform TrustManager at runtime so the app accepts the interception proxy's certificate, exposing API traffic for testing.
pairs.b: Frida script to defeat SSL pinning on Android apps: override okhttp3.CertificatePinner check() and the X509TrustManager so pinned connections trust Burp's CA, letting testers intercept the app's HTTPS requests.

pairs.label: DISTINCT
pairs.a: Bypassing Android certificate pinning with Frida. Hook OkHttp3 CertificatePinner.check and the platform TrustManager at runtime so the app accepts the interception proxy's certificate.
pairs.b: Bypassing Android root detection with Frida. Hook RootBeer isRooted() and File.exists checks for su binaries so the banking app runs on a rooted test device.

pairs.label: DUPLICATE
pairs.a: Exported Android activity without permission lets other apps launch internal screens. Any installed app can send an explicit intent to the exported settings activity and reach functionality meant to be protected, such as changing account details.
pairs.b: Insecure IPC: an activity declared android:exported=true with no permission can be started by a malicious app via an explicit Intent, opening a privileged internal screen that should only be reachable from inside the app.

pairs.label: DISTINCT
pairs.a: Exported Android activity without permission lets other apps launch internal screens via an explicit intent and reach privileged functionality.
pairs.b: Android app stores session tokens in plaintext SharedPreferences. Anyone with a backup or root access can read the XML file and reuse the token to take over the account.

pairs.label: DUPLICATE
pairs.a: Server-side request forgery in a PDF export feature. The renderer fetches attacker-supplied image URLs, so pointing it at http://169.254.169.254/ returns cloud instance metadata and IAM credentials.
pairs.b: SSRF through HTML-to-PDF conversion: injected tags make the server request internal addresses, including the AWS metadata endpoint, leaking temporary credentials in the generated PDF.

pairs.label: DISTINCT
pairs.a: Server-side request forgery in a PDF export feature. The renderer fetches attacker-supplied image URLs and leaks cloud metadata credentials.
pairs.b: Path traversal in a file download endpoint. The filename parameter is joined to the upload directory without normalisation, so ../../etc/passwd reads arbitrary files from the server.

pairs.label: DUPLICATE
pairs.a: iOS deep link handler opens arbitrary URLs in an in-app WKWebView with a JavaScript bridge. A crafted myapp:// link loads an attacker page that calls the bridge to read the user's auth token.
pairs.b: Custom URL scheme abuse on iOS: the app's deep link loads any supplied URL into a WKWebView that exposes a native message handler, so a malicious link can run JavaScript that steals the session token through the bridge.

pairs.label: DISTINCT
pairs.a: iOS deep link handler opens arbitrary URLs in an in-app WKWebView with a JavaScript bridge, letting a crafted link steal the auth token.
pairs.b: iOS app disables App Transport Security with NSAllowsArbitraryLoads, so API calls fall back to plain HTTP and can be read and modified on a shared Wi-Fi network.

pairs.label: DUPLICATE
pairs.a: Insecure deserialization in a Java endpoint that accepts serialized objects. Sending a ysoserial CommonsCollections gadget chain results in remote code execution as the application user.
pairs.b: Java object deserialization of untrusted input: the service calls readObject on request bodies, and a Commons Collections gadget built with ysoserial executes arbitrary commands on the server.

pairs.label: DISTINCT
pairs.a: Insecure deserialization in a Java endpoint that accepts serialized objects; a ysoserial gadget chain gives remote code execution.
pairs.b: Server-side template injection in a Java app using FreeMarker. User input reaches the template, and the ?new built-in instantiates freemarker.template.utility.Execute to run commands.

pairs.label: DUPLICATE
pairs.a: OAuth redirect_uri validation only checks the prefix, so https://app.example.com.attacker.net is accepted and the authorization code is sent to the attacker, allowing account takeover.
pairs.b: Account takeover via loose OAuth redirect validation: the provider matches redirect_uri with startsWith, letting an attacker-controlled domain that begins with the legitimate host receive victims' authorization codes.

pairs.label: DISTINCT
pairs.a: OAuth redirect_uri validation only checks the prefix, so an attacker domain receives the authorization code, allowing account takeover.
pairs.b: JWT accepted with alg set to none. The API skips signature verification when the header says none, so a forged token with any user id is accepted.

pairs.label: DUPLICATE
pairs.a: Stored XSS in a markdown comment renderer. Links using a javascript: scheme survive sanitisation and run in the viewer's session when clicked, stealing CSRF tokens.
pairs.b: Markdown sanitiser allows javascript: URLs in links, giving persistent cross-site scripting in comments that executes for any user who clicks the link.

pairs.label: DISTINCT
pairs.a: Stored XSS in a markdown comment renderer via javascript: links that survive sanitisation.
pairs.b: SQL injection in the comment search filter. The sort parameter is concatenated into ORDER BY, allowing boolean-based blind extraction of the users table.

pairs.label: DUPLICATE
pairs.a: Web cache deception: requesting /account/settings/nonexistent.css returns the private account page, and the CDN caches it because of the .css extension, so an attacker can later fetch the victim's cached data.
pairs.b: Cache deception via path confusion. Appending a static-looking suffix such as .css to an authenticated URL makes the origin serve personal data while the cache stores it as a public static file for anyone to retrieve.

pairs.label: DISTINCT
pairs.a: Web cache deception: a static-looking suffix on an authenticated URL makes the CDN cache private account pages for anyone to read.
pairs.b: CORS misconfiguration reflects any Origin and sets Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, so an attacker site can read authenticated API responses from the victim's browser.

pairs.label: DUPLICATE
pairs.a: Android WebView with setJavaScriptEnabled and addJavascriptInterface loads untrusted URLs from an intent extra, so a malicious app can open a page that calls exposed Java methods.
pairs.b: WebView JavaScript interface exposed to attacker content: the app loads a URL passed in an Intent into a WebView that registers addJavascriptInterface, letting injected JavaScript invoke native app methods.

pairs.label: DISTINCT
pairs.a: Android WebView with addJavascriptInterface loads untrusted URLs from an intent extra, exposing native methods to attacker JavaScript.
pairs.b: Android content provider exported without read permission exposes the app's SQLite database, and a projection parameter allows SQL injection from another installed app.

pairs.label: DUPLICATE
pairs.a: Prototype pollution in a Node.js merge utility. A JSON body with __proto__.isAdmin set to true pollutes Object.prototype, granting admin access to every subsequent request.
pairs.b: Polluting Object.prototype through a recursive merge of user JSON: sending {"__proto__": {"isAdmin": true}} makes every object inherit isAdmin, bypassing authorisation checks in the Node.js API.

pairs.label: DISTINCT
pairs.a: Prototype pollution in a Node.js merge utility lets __proto__.isAdmin grant admin access.
pairs.b: Node.js package typosquat on npm installs a postinstall script that exfiltrates environment variables and SSH keys from developer machines.

pairs.label: DUPLICATE
pairs.a: iOS app stores the user's PIN and refresh token in NSUserDefaults instead of the Keychain, so they can be read from an unencrypted device backup.
pairs.b: Sensitive data in NSUserDefaults on iOS: the refresh token and passcode are saved to the app's plist rather than the Keychain, exposing them to anyone with access to an iTunes backup.

pairs.label: DISTINCT
pairs.a: iOS app stores the user's PIN and refresh token in NSUserDefaults instead of the Keychain.
pairs.b: iOS jailbreak detection bypass with Frida: hook fileExistsAtPath for Cydia paths and canOpenURL for cydia:// so the app runs on a jailbroken device.

pairs.label: DUPLICATE
pairs.a: GraphQL introspection left enabled in production reveals hidden admin mutations, and the deleteUser mutation lacks authorisation checks.
pairs.b: Exposed GraphQL schema via introspection lists undocumented admin mutations; calling deleteUser works for ordinary users because the resolver never checks roles.

pairs.label: DISTINCT
pairs.a: GraphQL introspection reveals hidden admin mutations that lack authorisation checks.
pairs.b: GraphQL batching attack: sending hundreds of login mutations in one request bypasses the per-request rate limit and allows password brute forcing.

pairs.label: DUPLICATE
pairs.a: Race condition in a coupon redemption endpoint. Sending many parallel requests in a single packet redeems the same single-use code multiple times before the database marks it used.
pairs.b: Limit overrun via the single-packet attack: concurrent requests to apply a one-time discount code all pass the check before the update commits, so the coupon is applied repeatedly.

pairs.label: DISTINCT
pairs.a: Race condition in a coupon redemption endpoint lets a single-use code be redeemed multiple times with parallel requests.
pairs.b: Insecure direct object reference in the order API: changing the numeric orderId returns other customers' invoices and addresses.

pairs.label: DUPLICATE
pairs.a: Android app's Firebase Realtime Database rules allow public read, so the hard-coded database URL in the APK gives anyone access to all user records.
pairs.b: Misconfigured Firebase: the database URL extracted from the decompiled APK accepts unauthenticated .json reads, dumping every user's profile data.

pairs.label: DISTINCT
pairs.a: Android app's Firebase Realtime Database rules allow public read, exposing all user records.
pairs.b: Hard-coded AWS access keys in an Android APK's strings.xml give write access to the company's S3 bucket.

pairs.label: DUPLICATE
pairs.a: Password reset poisoning via the Host header. The reset email link is built from the request Host header, so an attacker triggers a reset for the victim with Host set to their domain and captures the token.
pairs.b: Host header injection in forgot-password: the application uses the supplied Host to build the reset URL, sending the victim a link to the attacker's server that leaks the reset token.

pairs.label: DISTINCT
pairs.a: Password reset poisoning via the Host header leaks reset tokens to the attacker's domain.
pairs.b: Password reset tokens are predictable because they are an MD5 of the email and timestamp, so an attacker can compute a valid token for any user.
